strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems security
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (MMLU, Alpaca, Samsum, Chatdoctor), LLM models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-v3), and attack types
Consistent improvements over baselines (3-7%) with well-organized presentation and clear motivation
Ablation study validates the importance of the backpropagation component; temporal DAG construction is technically sound
Tests both fixed and dynamic MAS topologies, demonstrating robustness across different system configurations
weaknesses: Circular dependency in methodology: using an external LLM to detect compromised LLMs is questionable—if the evaluator LLM can be misled or compromised, the entire defense fails, but this vulnerability is not adequately addressed

Limited novelty: approach primarily combines existing techniques (temporal DAGs, PageRank aggregation, LLM-based scoring) without significant innovation; core contribution is engineering rather than methodological advance

Detection rate caveats undermine claims: 93% detection with caveat that 7% undetected cases result in blocking 'severely affected agents' is circular logic—may harm benign agents and degrade system functionality

Oversimplified design choices: ternary contribution scoring {-1, 0, 1} lacks justification for why this coarse discretization captures attack patterns; threshold ε=1.5 chosen empirically without sensitivity analysis or principled guidance for practitioners
Incomplete adversarial evaluation: no assessment against adaptive attacks where adversaries know the defense mechanism; missing evaluation against zero-day exploits or naturally-occurring failures

Small-scale and limited analysis: experiments use only 100 samples per MMLU subdomain and 5-7 agents; scalability to larger MAS unclear; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; metrics lack precision/recall/F1 for misclassification analysis

'Dynamic' graph experiments are poorly defined and under-developed—unclear how topology changes differ fundamentally from sequential attacks; results show minimal performance difference from static case
Missing computational complexity analysis and overhead assessment; method requires multiple LLM calls per detection cycle which may be computationally expensive relative to baseline defenses
Backward propagation lacks rigorous justification beyond PageRank similarity; initialization strategy for intermediate nodes unclear; no exploration of alternative aggregation functions

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem of defending LLM-based multi-agent systems against corruption attacks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, models, and attack types with consistent improvements (3-7% on benchmarks, up to 16% on modification attacks)
Novel dynamic defense capability supporting graph restructuring, contrasting with static defenses in prior work
Extensive experimental details and promised code release support reproducibility
Clear presentation of experimental setup with detailed prompts and hyperparameter specifications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is essentially PageRank-like backward propagation on MAS graphs with LLM-based edge scoring—the paper itself acknowledges resemblance to PageRank
Critical assumption that attacks succeed ONLY when edge score equals 1 is overly restrictive and lacks justification; real attacks may operate through multiple patterns
Circular logic flaw: method relies on independent LLM for edge scoring but provides no explanation for why this external evaluator is immune to attacks that fool the main MAS LLMs

Inadequate treatment of 7% detection failures; the claim that 'detected agents are those most severely affected by the attack' raises concerns about removing benign agents and is not properly analyzed
Threshold selection (ε=1.5) lacks principled justification; no sensitivity analysis provided for choosing thresholds in new scenarios
Initialization in Eq. 1 is problematic: nodes receive ±1 scores based on agreement with final decision, but successfully corrupted benign agents would appear as agreement despite maliciousness

Attack scenarios are limited to simple prompt-based manipulations; missing evaluation against sophisticated attacks (data poisoning, adaptive attacks designed to evade the detector, fine-tuning attacks)
No theoretical guarantees on detection accuracy, false-positive rates, or robustness characterization; no formal analysis of why the approach should work
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: no error analysis, qualitative examples, or explanation of edge cases (multiple simultaneous corruptions, subtle attacks with all scores ≈0)
Experimental fairness concerns: G-Safeguard comparison doesn't account for computational costs and retraining requirements; limited baseline set with incomplete specifications
Figure 1 is cluttered and difficult to parse; mechanism explanation in Section 3.3 is hand-wavy without formal justification
Dynamic graph experiments lack clarity on how structure changes and agent selection occurs; misleading '88% → 88%' claim misrepresents identical values as showing minimal decline

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem: defending LLM-based MAS against corruption attacks with clear motivation for why existing static/local defenses are insufficient

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple dimensions: 2 LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), multiple datasets (MMLU, Alpaca, Samsum, ChatDoctor), multiple architectures (flat, hierarchical), 5+ attack types, both static and dynamic scenarios, plus ablation study

Strong and consistent empirical results: 3-7% improvements over baselines on multiple benchmarks, 91-95% detection accuracy, particularly strong on sophisticated 'Modification' attacks (16-10% vs baselines' 5-7%)

Clear problem articulation and intuitive methodology: Well-motivated dynamic graph repair paradigm with clear visualization; backward propagation approach elegantly captures both local and global information propagation
Solid reproducibility: detailed prompts in appendices, specific hyperparameters, public datasets/models, code promised; enables verification and follow-up work
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution (Eq. 1) is essentially PageRank on temporal DAGs—a straightforward algorithmic adaptation rather than novel methodology; signed graph with discrete {-1,0,1} scoring is intuitive but conceptually simple

Critical unanalyzed dependency on external LLM for edge scoring: No evaluation of scoring LLM's reliability, accuracy, or robustness; if scoring LLM is unreliable or attacked, entire defense fails; discrete scoring oversimplifies nuanced agreement; creates hidden vulnerability

Ad-hoc threshold selection without sensitivity analysis: ε=1.5 chosen because 'performs best' with no explanation of derivation, distribution, or sensitivity analysis; raises serious concerns about generalization to new domains and robustness of methodology

Inadequate analysis of detection failures: 7% undetected cases dismissed as 'agents most severely affected by attack'; lacks false positive/negative rate analysis; removing severely-affected benign agents could be harmful; no consequences analysis

Weak theoretical justification: Mechanism explanation (Sec 3.3) is informal; why should extreme scores indicate malicious agents? No formal analysis, theoretical guarantees, or conditions for correctness of detection; appears heuristic rather than principled

Limited scalability demonstration: All experiments use small MAS (5-7 agents); scalability to 50+ agents unexplored; computational cost analysis missing despite claiming efficiency; number of expensive LLM API calls per edge not addressed

Vague dynamic graph experimental setup: Section 4.3 lacks detail on how graph changes are implemented, frequency, and total number; limits reproducibility and transparency of dynamic scenario evaluation
Single-attacker limitation: All experiments assume one malicious agent; multiple coordinated attackers not tested; real attack scenarios often involve sophisticated multi-agent coordination

Artificial attack injection: Prompt-based behavior modification may not represent real attacks (model weight manipulation, trojanized models); limits adversarial realism and threat model applicability

strengths: Addresses a critical and timely security problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems with clear practical motivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple LLM models, MAS architectures, datasets, attack types, and realistic adaptive attacks
Strong empirical results: >90% detection accuracy, 3-7% task accuracy improvement, and particularly robust performance (10-16% advantage) on semantic modification attacks where baselines fail
Practical design advantages: training-free query-level detection, single-pass efficiency (~10% overhead), adaptive to dynamic topologies, and interpretable contribution scoring
Thorough evaluation methodology including human-LLM alignment studies (96-98% accuracy), scalability analysis, dynamic graph experiments, and ablation studies
Clear presentation with informative figures and comprehensive tables demonstrating strong empirical performance across diverse dimensions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core algorithm is a straightforward application of row-normalized matrix propagation on DAGs, with connection to PageRank revealing non-innovative foundations

Critical architectural vulnerability: entire defense depends on an external LLM scorer to determine edge signs; Sections 4.6-4.7 show 3-4% performance degradation under system-aware adaptive attacks targeting the scorer, and monitor accuracy drops to 81-82%

Empirically-tuned threshold parameter ε lacks principled justification; sensitivity analysis (Figures 2-3) shows sharp accuracy variations (84-87%) across ε ∈ [1.3-1.7], requiring domain-specific tuning that contradicts 'no training required' claim
Synchronous DAG formulation limits applicability: assumes fixed temporal rounds and rules out asynchronous/cyclic communication patterns common in real-world MAS; generalizability unclear

Incomplete threat model: limited to single-agent compromises in thorough evaluation; coordinated multi-agent attacks and Byzantine thresholds acknowledged as out-of-scope without clear formal definition of resilience bounds
Evaluation scope limited to small systems (5-7 agents, 3-5 rounds) with specific task types (QA and text generation); computational overhead grows to 8.74% for larger configurations
Formal theoretical gaps: no proof of detection correctness, no characterization of attack classes BPD can provably detect, and false positive/negative trade-offs not quantified or analyzed

Terminal condition definition unclear: paper does not explicitly explain how final answer is determined in Flat structures where multiple agents propose different answers, affecting interpretation of Eq. (6)

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem in LLM-based multi-agent system security with practical motivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple MAS topologies, attack types, datasets, and model backbones with careful ablation studies
Clear and interpretable methodology: signed DAG formulation with backward propagation is straightforward to understand and implement
No training requirement enables adaptation to dynamic MAS without retraining, providing practical advantage over graph-based baselines
Efficient in practice with only 9-10% computational overhead while maintaining strong detection accuracy (90%+)
Strong empirical results on standard attacks with consistent improvements (3-7% task accuracy gains, 10% on modification attacks)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: modeling MAS as temporal DAG and backward propagation is straightforward application of standard graph algorithms; LLM-based edge scoring is not novel

Critical single point of failure in scoring mechanism f(sᵢ,sⱼ)∈{-1,0,1}: reliability validated on only 50 samples (Table 21); System-Aware adaptive attacks reduce monitor accuracy to 81-82% (Table 13), demonstrating the mechanism is learnable and exploitable

Ad-hoc threshold hyperparameter (ε=1.5): Figures 2-3 show strong sensitivity with 84%→87%→82% accuracy as ε ranges 1.3→1.5→1.7; no principled method for new domains, contradicting claimed adaptivity to evolving attacks

Weak threat model: core assumption that malicious agents have substantially different contribution scores is not formally justified; no analysis of coordinated attacks or intermediate-score adversaries; Byzantine threshold attacks explicitly acknowledged as out-of-scope

Overstated claims about dynamic performance: abstract claims method 'preserves static-graph performance' but Table 7 shows non-trivial drops (89%→88% Flat, 87%→85% Hierarchy); claim of adaptivity undermined by ε tuning requirement

Experimental setup favors proposed method: attacks are relatively simple and synthetically defined; scoring prompt explicitly trains with -1/0/1 semantics unrealistic for real judges; baselines show surprisingly poor performance; no evaluation on authentic MAS tasks

Insufficient robustness analysis: System-Aware adaptive attacks achieve 81-82% monitor accuracy (~18% evasion rate); author explanation that 'easily misled agents' are isolated is circular reasoning when goal is accurate attacker detection; only 2 compatible combined attack combinations tested

Lack of theoretical foundation: no formal analysis of when/why contribution scores identify malicious agents; no Byzantine fault tolerance characterization; no study of attack coordination or failure modes; backward propagation assumes edge score independence

Crude graph repair mechanism: removing all edges from detected agents lacks nuance; no analysis of false positive impact on system functionality; hierarchical systems could be destroyed by removing advisor edges
Incomplete error analysis: insufficient breakdown of detection false positives vs. false negatives across attack types; limited characterization of which scenarios evade detection
Coarse-grained scoring: ternary {-1,0,1} lacks nuance for partial agreement; no gradation of influence strength
Reproducibility concerns: code repository incompletely referenced; LLM scoring is stochastic with no variance analysis; prompt engineering details relegated to appendix
Missing scalability evaluation: tests limited to 10 agents/5 rounds; unclear behavior for large MAS (100+ agents); no time complexity analysis

strengths: Addresses timely and critical problem of corruption attack defense in LLM-based multi-agent systems with practical relevance for deployed systems
Novel signed DAG formulation combined with elegant backward propagation mechanism for global agent influence analysis; connection to PageRank is well-motivated

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple architectures (Flat, Hierarchical), LLM backbones (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), attack types (5 variants), dynamic scenarios, adaptive attacks, and combined attacks
Strong empirical results: >90% detection accuracy, 3-7% task accuracy improvements, particularly effective on semantic modification attacks (+10-16%), with minimal 9-10% time overhead
Practical advantage over baselines: requires no offline training, enabling immediate adaptability to new MAS topologies and evolving attacks
Rigorous evaluation including system-aware adaptive attacks and ablation studies demonstrating necessity of backward propagation component
Excellent presentation with clear figures, detailed algorithm description, comprehensive appendices, and reproducibility standards; promised code release
weaknesses: Critical reliance on external LLM scorer for edge weight assignment {-1,0,1}; while Table B.4 claims 96-98% human alignment, validation limited to 50 samples and doesn't capture subtle semantic disagreements; adaptive scoring attacks (Section 4.6) show vulnerability with 6% detection accuracy drop

Limited theoretical analysis: no formal guarantees on detection conditions, characterization of defendable attack classes, or why Δ(i) metric effectively identifies attackers; malicious agents could potentially craft scores to match majority deviations

Scalability concerns: experiments limited to 10 agents and 5 dialogue rounds; DAG memory complexity O(nT) not analyzed; no evaluation on real-world large-scale systems; unclear performance with varying agent counts across rounds

Terminal initialization (Eq. 6) assumption only validates against final answer match, potentially failing when partially successful attacks build misleading consensus; validity not discussed across different task types

Hyperparameter ϵ requires empirical tuning; agent-level aggregation uses simple averaging vulnerable to attacks targeting specific rounds; no principled method for practitioners to select ϵ in new domains
All attacks are programmatically implemented; no human-crafted adversarial examples or evaluation against attackers with full knowledge of defense mechanisms before attack launch
Generalization concerns: evaluation limited to multiple-choice QA and text generation; applicability to code generation, planning, or tasks with subjective correctness undefined
Acknowledged limitation that Byzantine-threshold-exceeding attacks are out-of-scope (Section 4.7) deserves more prominent discussion and formal characterization

DAG formulation assumes synchronous communication; alternative graph formalisms (hypergraphs, heterogeneous graphs) not compared; mitigation strategy (complete edge removal) is crude without performance-security trade-off analysis
